what_its_for: Taliglucerase alfa is used to treat a condition called Gaucher disease type 1. In Gaucher disease, your body does not have enough of a certain enzyme (a protein that helps break things down). This causes fatty substances to build up in your organs, like your liver, spleen, and bone marrow, causing pain, swelling, and other problems. This medicine replaces the missing enzyme so your body can work more normally.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly injected into your vein through a needle or catheter. A healthcare provider — such as a nurse or doctor — will give you this infusion in a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. Each infusion session usually takes about 60 to 120 minutes. You will be monitored during and after the infusion for any reactions. Do not try to give this medicine to yourself at home unless your doctor has specifically trained you and approved it.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight. The usual starting dose is 60 units per kilogram (units/kg) of body weight, given once every 2 weeks. Your doctor may adjust your dose up or down depending on how well you are responding to treatment. Always follow your doctor's dosing schedule exactly.
missed_dose: If you miss or have to reschedule your infusion appointment, contact your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible to set up a new appointment. Try not to go too long between infusions. Do not try to 'catch up' by doubling your dose.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals. If you are storing it at home (only if instructed by your doctor), keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in its original packaging and out of direct light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Once the medicine has been mixed (reconstituted) and diluted, it should be used within 24 hours if kept in the refrigerator.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting this medication. There are no specific foods or drinks known to interact with taliglucerase alfa. Avoid missing your scheduled infusion appointments, as consistent treatment is important for managing Gaucher disease.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following during or after your infusion: trouble breathing or shortness of breath, chest tightness or pain, dizziness or feeling faint, fast or pounding heartbeat, sudden rash, hives, or itching, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, fever or chills, nausea or vomiting, headache, or back or joint pain. These could be signs of an allergic reaction or infusion-related reaction. Also call your doctor if you notice any new or worsening symptoms of Gaucher disease, such as increased bone pain, unusual bruising or bleeding, or unusual tiredness.
when_it_works: You may not notice improvements right away. Some people begin to see changes — like reduced swelling of the liver or spleen or improved blood counts — within a few months of starting treatment. Bone pain and bone-related changes may take longer to improve, sometimes up to 1 to 2 years. It is important to keep all of your follow-up appointments so your doctor can track your progress with regular blood tests, imaging, and physical exams.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of this medicine during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been fully studied. Your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. Children: This medicine can be used in children 4 years of age and older. Doses are based on the child's weight. Older Adults: This medicine can be used in older adults. Your doctor will monitor you closely for any side effects. Allergies: Tell your doctor if you have ever had a reaction to this medicine, similar enzyme replacement medicines, or any of its ingredients.
